title: Appeals Court Rejects Trump's Bid to Revive $100,000 H-1B Visa Fee
excerpt: The 1st Circuit Court of Appeals declined to halt a lower court ruling that struck down the fee as an unlawful tax, delivering another blow to the administration's immigration crackdown.
body:
• The 1st U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals declined to stay a June 8 ruling that struck down the $100,000 H-1B visa fee as an unlawful tax.
  • The fee, imposed by presidential proclamation in September 2025, raised H-1B costs from roughly $2,000-$5,000 to over $100,000.
  • A separate challenge by the U.S. Chamber of Commerce in Washington, D.C., remains pending before the D.C. Circuit.
  • The ruling offers relief to tech companies and healthcare employers that depend heavily on H-1B workers.

What the Court Decided

A federal appeals court on Friday rejected the Trump administration's emergency bid to revive the $100,000 fee on new H-1B visa applications, leaving in place a lower court order that declared the charge an unlawful tax.

https://x.com/Reuters/status/2080830450440794485

The Boston-based 1st U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals declined to put on hold U.S. District Judge Leo Sorokin's June 8 ruling, which concluded that the fee was not a lawful penalty but a tax that the president had no congressional authorization to impose. The decision marked the administration's second failed attempt to restore the fee through the courts.

"Here, the substance and application of the $100,000 payment reveal that it is a tax, regardless of what the payment is called."

— Judge Leo Sorokin, U.S. District Court

How the Fee Came to Be

President Trump issued Proclamation 10973 in September 2025, invoking his broad immigration powers under Sections 212(f) and 215(a) of the Immigration and Nationality Act. The order imposed a $100,000 supplemental payment on new H-1B petitions filed for workers located outside the United States. Before the proclamation, H-1B filing fees ranged from roughly $960 to $7,595 depending on the employer and filing circumstances.

The administration argued the fee was a monetary penalty meant to curb alleged abuse of the H-1B program and protect U.S. workers in STEM fields. Twenty Democratic state attorneys general challenged the proclamation in Massachusetts, arguing it exceeded presidential authority and violated the Administrative Procedure Act.

The Legal Landscape

The H-1B fee fight is playing out across multiple courts with contradictory outcomes. In December 2025, a federal judge in Washington, D.C., upheld the fee in a separate lawsuit brought by the U.S. Chamber of Commerce and the Association of American Universities. That case is currently before the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals, which heard oral arguments in March 2026.

A third challenge, filed by healthcare organizations and labor unions in California, remains pending in the Northern District of California. The Massachusetts ruling cited the Supreme Court's February 2026 decision striking down Trump's sweeping tariffs pursued under a national emergency law, finding the same logic applied to the visa fee.

Because the Massachusetts court temporarily stayed its own ruling during the appeal process, the $100,000 fee has remained in effect for new petitions filed through the State Department and USCIS. Friday's decision removes that stay, meaning the fee can no longer be collected under the Massachusetts ruling.

Impact on Employers and Workers

The H-1B program offers 65,000 visas annually, with an additional 20,000 for workers with advanced degrees, typically approved for three to six years. Technology companies are the heaviest users, but healthcare systems, universities and research institutions also depend on the program to fill specialized roles.

Industry groups have warned that the fee would effectively price many employers out of the program. The American Society for Clinical Pathology noted that the $100,000 charge would worsen existing shortages in pathology and clinical laboratory staffing, where international professionals fill critical gaps.

What Comes Next

The White House has signaled it will continue fighting. A spokesperson said the administration is confident the ruling will be reversed, calling the H-1B program a system that "has been abused for decades." The outcome at the D.C. Circuit, where a different judge upheld the fee, could create a circuit split that escalates the issue to the Supreme Court.

For Indian professionals, who account for roughly 70% of all H-1B visas issued annually, the case has outsized stakes. A permanent reinstatement of the fee would dramatically raise the cost of working in the United States and could push more employers toward alternative visa categories or offshore arrangements.
